name: Poets, Painters and Rhythms of Latin America
description: From a Maya book of creation to Despacito: the writers, artists and musicians who made Latin America's culture heard around the world.

checkpoints.name: Old voices, new nations
checkpoints.note: The Popol Vuh, a Maya story of creation, is set down in writing in the sixteenth century. In the 1800s Mexico, Argentina and Brazil become independent countries, and around 1880 the tango takes shape in the port cities of the Río de la Plata.

checkpoints.name: Revolution and verse
checkpoints.note: The Mexican Revolution begins in 1910 and shapes Frida Kahlo's world; she paints The Two Fridas in 1939. Jorge Luis Borges in Buenos Aires and Pablo Neruda in Chile write works that change Spanish-language literature, and Celia Cruz, born in Cuba in 1925, grows up with the island's music.

checkpoints.name: Boom and bossa
checkpoints.note: The Cuban Revolution triumphs in 1959, and Celia Cruz leaves the island in 1960. In Brazil, bossa nova (1958) and The Girl from Ipanema (1962) make a gentle samba famous worldwide. Gabriel García Márquez publishes One Hundred Years of Solitude in 1967, and Latin American fiction finds readers across the globe.

checkpoints.name: Old masters, new readers
checkpoints.note: Pablo Neruda wins the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1971 and García Márquez in 1982. Paulo Coelho's The Alchemist (1988) becomes a world bestseller, and in the 1990s the veteran Cuban musicians of the Buena Vista Social Club record an album that reaches listeners far beyond Havana.

checkpoints.name: Screens and streams
checkpoints.note: City of God (2002) shows life in the favelas of Rio, and Pan's Labyrinth (2006) mixes fairy tale with the Spanish Civil War era. Despacito (2017) becomes one of the most streamed songs in the world, showing how far Latin pop now travels.
